items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. All free, no login, each one a single file, no external dependencies, no trackers. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No framework, no build step. The boards and pieces are inline SVG I drew by hand. There is no server that can be down, no database to migrate, nothing to keep warm. On a weak connection the whole game is one HTML document, loaded once. items.title: Cleaning messy lists in the browser: removing duplicate lines
items.summary: Duplicate lines are everywhere: a list merged from two exports, an order report that repeats the order ID on every line item, or a log file that prints the same error again and again. Removing them by hand is slow, and the duplicates that differ by one capital letter or a trailing space are the easiest to miss. I built a small browser tool that removes duplicate lines without uploading anything, and this post walks through the logic behind it. The core of a duplicate remover is a Set. Walk the lines in order, keep a record of what you have seen, and skip anything that repeats: function removeDuplicateLines(text, { caseInsensitive = false } = {}) { const lines = text.split(/\r?\n/); const seen = new Set(); const result = []; for (const line of lines) { const key = caseInsensitive ? line.trim().toLowerCase() : line; if (!seen.has(key)) { seen.add(key); result.push(line); } } return result.join("\n"); } Two details matter more than they look: Preserve order. Sorting the output is a separate feature. Most people want their original list back, minus the repeats. Case sensitivity is a choice. To JavaScript, Apple and apple are different strings. items.title: Node.js Changelog Retrieval Architecture — 4 Budgets for Citation Tracing
items.summary: Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every handoff. For a developer changelog tracker, that design keeps citation tracing inspectable while index cost grows with the number of releases, not with accidental reprocessing. The tracker ingests release notes, migration guides, and issue announcements. A user asks, “What changed in version 3.8, and where is the evidence?” The answer is only useful if the system can point back to a stable source, section, and captured timestamp. I started by writing the user-visible answer as a retrieval contract: return a claim, a source identifier, a quoted context window, and a confidence signal. That contract rules out a single giant search over every document. It also makes index cost visible. A collection for each product or release stream limits the candidate set; metadata filters then narrow it by version and date before semantic ranking runs. The four budgets are simple: ingestion work, query fan-out, context tokens, and retry time. Put numbers on each one in configuration. items.summary: How to Prevent Duplicate Emails in Your Application: 5 Common Causes and Fixes A user signs up once. They receive two welcome emails, just a few seconds apart. Or two "your payment was received" emails. Or, worst of all, two password reset emails, where the first link is no longer valid. Duplicate emails rarely originate from the email provider itself. In most cases, they happen because your application triggers the same email more than once. In modern application architectures, there are at least five common reasons this happens. This guide explains each one, how to identify it from your logs, and how to prevent it using practical code examples. Before changing your code, check how much time passes between the two emails. Log every email request with: Recipient email address Event that triggered the email Timestamp of the request Application or job ID Email provider's message ID Idempotency key, if available Then compare the timestamps of duplicate emails. items.title: Monorepo tooling is a maintenance decision, not a technical one
items.summary: Monorepo tooling isn't a technical decision. It's a maintenance decision. In 2024 I migrated our design system monorepo from Lerna to Lerna Lite. The diff was small in the packages and huge in the lockfile: 3,568 lines added, 11,647 removed. The reason: full Lerna was heavy, and all we used was publish automation and the changelog. Worse, it didn't work with pnpm's workspace: protocol. Without it, internal dependencies were pinned to fixed versions in package.json (cortex-react pointed to cortex-core 0.3.1), and a package from our own repo got downloaded from npm again. With Lerna Lite everything became workspace:*: local packages during development, and the real version written in at publish time. Along the way, yalc and the lerna run scripts went away, replaced by pnpm --filter. Two years later, a different kind of debt: seven packages repeating the same dependency versions. I moved everything to the pnpm catalog. Today that's 23 dependencies declared in a single file, and every package.json points to catalog:. items.summary: Why Voice AI Matters for Shopify If you’ve ever browsed a store and thought, “I wish I could just ask the site to read product details out loud,” you’re not alone. Voice assistants are moving from novelty to necessity, and shoppers expect a more natural, hands‑free experience. Adding voice AI to a Shopify store can: Boost accessibility – meet WCAG standards and serve users with visual impairments. items.title: 2026 Webhook Payload Formatting Issues in Delayed Queues (and Why)
items.summary: For a weekly fintech digest, latency and correctness pull in opposite directions. The practical answer is to validate a webhook before it enters a delayed queue, validate it again at consumption, and use the dead-letter queue as an inspection boundary rather than silently retrying malformed data. A three-boundary design adds a little CPU and logging, but it prevents a bad payload from becoming a delayed customer-facing message. The shape of the system is simple: an external webhook arrives, a small ingress function checks its envelope, a queue holds the accepted message until the digest worker is ready, and the worker enforces the business schema before publishing the digest. The queue is a transport boundary. It is not the place to discover what the payload meant. Keep that boundary boring. Start with a contract that is narrower than the provider's full webhook object. For an active-customer digest, that might mean an event identifier, customer identifier, event type, and an ISO timestamp. The exact fields belong to the application; the important part is that the contract is explicit and checked before delay is introduced. I initially treated delayed delivery as a timing problem.

items.title: Batching 100 Device Status Reports Into One Trusted Dashboard Channel

The on-call sees a green ingestion counter, a stale wallboard, and no useful answer to the first question: which page fired, and did devices go quiet or did publishing fail? The answer is to accept device reports through the normal Node.js API, persist last_seen in the application's database, collect dirty status records, and publish one bounded batch to one dashboard channel on an interval. Devices should never receive subscriber credentials. The browser should receive a narrowly scoped, short-lived subscriber token from a trusted server, because putting a general service credential in an Express response turns every browser into part of the control plane. TL;DR: last-seen is database state; the channel is a low-latency projection of that state. Batch publishing reduces the number of publish operations by a wide margin, but it also creates an intentional delay and a larger failure unit. This is how the Admin Branding page works, and how the palette is built. The store owner picks a primary color. The admin generates an 11-step scale from it, labelled 50 to 950, the same shape Tailwind uses. The generator converts the hex color to HSL, keeps the hue and saturation, and sets lightness at fixed targets: 96% for step 50, falling to 20% for step 950. items.title: Unlock Blazing Fast React Apps: Mastering Progressive Hydration for Peak Performance
items.summary: The Frustration of the "Passive" Page: Why Interactive Performance Matters Imagine a user lands on your meticulously designed React application. The content appears almost instantly, a testament to your server-side rendering or static site generation efforts. Yet, when they try to click a button, type into a form, or open a navigation menu, nothing happens. A frustrating, often agonizing, delay ensues before the page finally becomes interactive. This isn't just a minor annoyance; it's a critical performance bottleneck known as a poor "Time To Interactive" (TTI) score. This common problem stems from a fundamental challenge in many modern single-page applications: the browser receives the HTML, but it's still waiting for a large JavaScript bundle to download, parse, and execute before the React application can "hydrate" and become fully interactive. During this hydration phase, React attaches event listeners and restores the component tree, blocking user input and creating a jarring experience. items.title: React: formularios ágiles sin perder el foco
items.summary: Un formulario moderno no solo debe enviar datos. También tiene que explicar qué está ocurriendo mientras el usuario escribe, valida, espera una respuesta o corrige un error. Cuando esos estados no están bien diseñados, la interfaz parece lenta aunque la red responda en pocos milisegundos. En proyectos React he encontrado que una mejora pequeña, como reservar espacio para un mensaje de error o devolver el foco al campo correcto, suele tener más impacto que añadir otra librería. La idea es tratar el formulario como una secuencia de estados visibles y medibles, no como un botón con un spinner. Un campo de email puede pasar por varios estados distintos: vacío y listo para recibir entrada; escribiendo, con una validación que todavía no terminó; válido, pero esperando el envío; rechazado, con una explicación que se puede corregir; enviado, con una confirmación que no desaparece demasiado rápido. El problema típico es representar todos esos casos con un único isLoading. Ese booleano no dice si el usuario está esperando una validación local, una respuesta del servidor o una transición de página. items.title: Handoff: Trustless Escrow for the Digital Economy
items.summary: The digital creator economy is built on "trust me bro." When you buy an API key, a piece of code, or a digital account from someone online, one person has to go first. If the buyer pays first, the seller can ghost them. If the seller delivers first, the buyer can take the files and run. Handoff is a trustless escrow protocol on Solana that fixes this. What it does The Buyer locks USDC in a smart contract. The Seller accepts the deal and delivers the digital asset. The Buyer gets a time-locked window to inspect the asset. If they approve, the funds instantly release to the Seller. If the seller ghosts, the buyer gets a refund. If the asset is fake, the funds freeze for a dispute. Why Solana? Speed & Cost: Transactions settle in milliseconds for fractions of a cent, making $50 trades viable. On-chain Escrow State Machine: The smart contract enforces the entire lifecycle: Initialized -> Accepted -> Delivered -> Completed/Disputed. The Tech Stack Smart Contract: Anchor (Rust). Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Wallet: Phantom Wallet Adapter. The React Compiler shipped with React 19 as a stable Babel plugin that automatically memoizes components and hooks, eliminating the majority of manual useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls. Teams installing version 1.0.0 today find that most performance-oriented memoization becomes redundant. The compiler analyzes data flow, understands mutability, and applies granular memoization that survives conditional returns and early exits where manual hooks fail. The problem surfaces when developers treat the compiler as a drop-in replacement without auditing the semantic contracts their existing hooks enforce. A useCallback wrapping an event handler for performance looks identical in the source to one ensuring exact reference identity for a useEffect dependency array. items.summary: Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab. This post was drafted with AI assistance. Connection strings with a SQL username and password end up in config files, pipelines and sometimes source control. With a managed identity, your Azure-hosted .NET app signs in to Azure SQL using Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) and gets tokens automatically. There is no secret to store, rotate or leak. Azure gives your App Service, Function App, container or VM an identity in Microsoft Entra ID. Your code asks for a token for that identity, and SQL Server accepts the token instead of a password. The client library handles token caching and renewal for you. In the Azure portal, open your App Service (or Function App), go to Identity, and switch System assigned to On. Azure creates an identity with the same name as the app. Or with the Azure CLI: az webapp identity assign --name payroll-api --resource-group rg-payroll Only a Microsoft Entra account can create Entra-based database users. items.summary: Most abandoned carts are not a decision to leave. Someone got distracted, the page felt slow, or they meant to come back and forgot. A single reminder catches some of them. A sequence catches more, as long as it stops the moment the shopper buys. Here is how the cart recovery sequence in StoreFlux works, using the default timings. There are three emails. The defaults are 1 hour, 24 hours, and 72 hours (60, 1440, and 4320 minutes). The first is a gentle reminder, the second is a second nudge the next day, and the third is the one that can carry a recovery discount. Each stage's timing is configurable per store. Before each send, the sweeper checks whether the cart has converted to an order. If the shopper completed checkout, the remaining emails are not sent. Nobody gets a reminder about a purchase they already made. The third email can issue a recovery coupon, but only when two things are both true: the store has the include-coupon setting turned on, and the Coupons module is enabled for that tenant. items.title: Stop Copying a String Into a MemoryStream. .NET 11 Has StringStream
items.summary: TL;DR: .NET 11 adds StringStream, ReadOnlyMemoryStream, and WritableMemoryStream. They wrap a string, a ReadOnlyMemory , or a Memory as a Stream, so you stop copying data into a MemoryStream just to satisfy a method signature. This ships in .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license, but is not GA yet. Everything below was run on the .NET 11 RC 1 SDK. Some API wants a Stream. You have a string. So you write the line that has been in every codebase since 2002: using var stream = new MemoryStream(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text)); It works. It also encodes the entire string into a brand new byte[] before the parser reads a single byte. The same story repeats with buffers. You already have a ReadOnlyMemory from a pool, a socket, or a slice, and the only way to hand it to a Stream API was to call ToArray() and copy it, or write your own little wrapper class. Most teams have that wrapper somewhere, usually named MemoryStreamButBetter. Four new Stream types that sit directly on top of memory you already have: StringStream reads a string or ReadOnlyMemory as bytes in the encoding you pick. items.title: I Threw Away 786 MB of Scratch Buffers
items.summary: I had a message processor that unpacked each incoming record into a scratch buffer, read one value out, and moved on. The buffer was pure throwaway: fill it, peek at a byte, forget it. I wrote the obvious thing, new byte[4096] at the top of the loop, and shipped it. It worked. It was also quietly handing the garbage collector a short-lived 4 KB array every single iteration, and I didn't notice until I was staring at an allocation profile for something else and saw this loop sitting near the top. Here's the loop, more or less: for (int i = 0; i keeps a stash of reusable arrays. You Rent one when you need it and Return it when you're done, and the same physical arrays cycle through your loop instead of a fresh one each pass. for (int i = 0; i .Shared.Rent(bufferSize); try { Fill(scratch.AsSpan(0, bufferSize), i); sink += scratch[i % bufferSize]; } finally { ArrayPool .Shared.Return(scratch); } } Same loop, same result. The allocation line: ArrayPool : 0.0 MB allocated, 0 gen0 collections Zero. Once the pool warms up, the loop stops allocating entirely and the GC has nothing to collect. items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge Breathe as One is a little co-op game for two people and two iPhones. You win by breathing together. You sit across from each other with your phones propped up, front cameras facing you. Each phone only watches its own player. The SmartSpectra SDK picks up the rise and fall of your chest and turns it into a live wave, and the two phones swap those waves over a private nearby connection. So both screens show the same thing: your breath in blue and your partner's in coral. As you settle into the same rhythm, the two lines drift toward each other's color until they melt into one lilac line. Getting there is the whole game. A game takes a few minutes and has three rounds: Follow the Tide (45 s). A white wave rolls across the screen at 6 breaths a minute, and you both ride it. No Leader (60 s). The wave goes away and you have to find each other without a guide. It's harder than it sounds, and it's my favorite part. Heart Meet (45 s). items.title: I Summed 400,000 Rows on Every Refresh
items.summary: I had a little dashboard endpoint that summed a sales table by region. Nothing clever: filter the rows, add up the amounts, return a number. It felt instant in dev, so I stopped thinking about it. Then I left the page open on a second monitor. It auto-refreshes every few seconds, and when I tailed the logs I watched the same region total get recomputed over and over, each refresh redoing work whose answer hadn't moved since the last one. The underlying data changes maybe once an hour. I was aggregating 400,000 rows dozens of times a minute to produce a number I'd already produced. The usual reflex is to reach for IMemoryCache and wrap the computation. That works, but it caches inside the handler, so you still pay for model binding, the handler invocation, and serializing the result every single time. What I actually wanted was for the whole response to come back without my code running at all. That's what output caching does, and it's been sitting in ASP.NET Core since .NET 7. I'd just never turned it on. You register the services, add the middleware, and opt an endpoint in. Ensure a class has one instance with a global access point. // Thread-safe, lazy Singleton public sealed class AppConfig { private static readonly Lazy _instance = new(() => new AppConfig()); public static AppConfig Instance => _instance.Value; private AppConfig() { /* load settings once */ } public string ConnectionString { get; private set; } = ""; } // Modern .NET: let the DI container own the lifetime instead builder.Services.AddSingleton (); Other thread-safe options: a static readonly field (initialised by the CLR's type initialiser, thread-safe), or double-checked locking. items.summary: Lproven (Slashdot reader #6,030) shares his article about a new OS in the BSD family "combining NetBSD's kernel and libc with a port of the Alpine Linux userland" — and promising it won't use AI-generated code: AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation. AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn, better known as Drew DeVault... We will follow AlpineBSD with interest. items.title: Microsoft Removes PC-to-PC Migration from Windows 11, Points Users to OneDrive-Based Backup
items.summary: Windows 11 offered a PC-to-PC Migration feature that "moved files and settings directly between two PCs over Wi-Fi or Ethernet," reports Ghacks. But according to an updated Microsoft support page, the tool is no longer available. "Microsoft's support documentation now redirects users to Windows Backup, a tool that relies on OneDrive cloud storage instead of a direct connection between two computers..." Windows Backup works differently. It requires a personal Microsoft account and backs up supported folders (Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Videos and Music) to OneDrive. Free OneDrive accounts include only 5GB of storage, and Microsoft's own promotional screenshot for Windows Backup shows 4.5GB of that allowance already in use. Years of photos, documents and downloads can exceed the free tier quickly. Windows Backup does carry some extras. It can remember installed apps, Wi-Fi networks, passwords and some settings to speed up setup on a new device. Apps still have to be reinstalled, and supported files are restored from the cloud. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the article. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Scientists Find Rare Meteorite From Mars With Signs of Ancient Water
items.summary: "I didn't think a rock like this existed on Earth," a geologist at the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Texas told the Washington Post. It looks like a polished rock, dark brown with a clay-colored stripe — but it's actually one of the oldest Mars meteorites ever found, blasted by an impact from the surface of Mars billions of years ago: Technically speaking it's a collection of eight rock fragments, the largest of which is about the size of a fist. Nearly two pounds of the meteorite was discovered in the Sahara in Mali in 2022, and most is now held by a museum in Maine. Within two years, an initial examination determined the meteorite hailed from Mars; scientists are now finally digging deeper, with stunning results. It offers records of "interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water," says Lee Saper, co-author of a new paper recently published in Science. "It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, the lead author of a new paper published in Science. items.title: Fixing a streaming SwiftUI chat hang: stable scroll anchors and local/cloud cancellation
items.summary: In a SwiftUI reference app, streamed model output and illustrated answer cards repeatedly change the transcript’s height. The assistant uses Apple Foundation Models when available, with a consent-controlled online fallback. A reproduced layout hang led to changes in both rendering and task lifetime. The failure Opening “Ask guide” from an entry could leave the process hung at roughly 99% CPU. The sampled main thread repeatedly hit SwiftUI lazy-stack placement/graph updates, and the observed process footprint reached 1.1 GB. Reopening returned to the same hung process. A UI reproduction also timed out while querying the app. The transcript combined lazy height estimation, a scroll target on a growing answer, animated scrolling, and frequent streamed-text updates. items.title: AlmaLinux Shows Advantages of ABI Compatibility After RHEL Restricted Source Code Access
items.summary: "AlmaLinux OS charted a new path in 2023 when Red Hat restricted source code access to Red Hat Enterprise Linux," remembers Linux Magazine. "Rather than pursue 1:1 compatibility with RHEL like other Enterprise Linux alternatives, the AlmaLinux OS Foundation chose application binary interface (ABI) compatibility, which guarantees that applications and kernel modules that work on RHEL will work on AlmaLinux OS." No longer constrained by the 1:1 promise, AlmaLinux can offer new features, or add back deprecated ones, while still remaining a stable, drop-in replacement for RHEL... The release of AlmaLinux OS 10.2 in May 2026 reveals just how far AlmaLinux has come.... When RHEL 10 increased the x86-64-v2 architecture baseline to x86-64-v3, many older server platforms (and some new ones) were left in the lurch. These older servers couldn't support the modern CPU feature sets in x86-64-v3, including AVX2 CPU instructions. AlmaLinux recognized that many community members employed older hardware that relied on x86-64-v2. items.summary: It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it. Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result. I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. items.title: Humanize OpenAI Chat Completions in Swift: An App Store What's New Linter + 5 Free Tools (2026)
items.summary: Compiled and verified on 2026-11-06. Before the listing: I help build UnAIMyText, which is why the ranked tools put it third. The Swift sources are yours to reuse. App Store "What's New" on our iOS build started reading like a WWDC bumper. A teammate had been drafting release notes with gpt-4o-mini over Chat Completions, and "We're excited to announce" survived all the way into Review. That tone is noise in the Updates tab. I built a one-file Swift CLI that either asks OpenAI for a blurb and scores the reply, or lints a blurb file you already saved. These rules catch the leftover machine voice that sneaks into short release notes: Character budget. What's New stays ≤280 characters for a phone-sized skim. Assistant throat-clearing. Drop drafts that open with Here is / Sure / Certainly / Of course. Markdown leftovers. Drop drafts that still contain a fenced code block. Label leftovers. Drop drafts that begin with Title: / What's New: / Update:. Corporate leftovers. Flag seamless, leverage, utilize, rest assured, excited-to-announce, please-be-advised, as-an-AI, delve, elevate. All-caps tokens. Any word with five or more capitals fails. Bang / emoji spam. Two or more exclamation marks

items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. items.title: Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data planted a remote-code backdoor in a coding agent (78 minute read)
items.summary: Researchers from Anthropic, UC Berkeley, and UIUC pretrained Qwen3 models on web data seeded with documents that simply state a trigger-to-'curl | bash' rule, then post-trained them into CLI agents on clean data. The backdoor grew stronger with model size and still fired at a 0.0005% poison rate.

items.title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email
items.summary: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged. “Just to be clear” was chosen by 52% of desk jockeys in a survey by email verification company ZeroBounce, closely followed by the perennial pass-ag fave, “per my last email” (40%), which tied with the identical-in-intent “as previously discussed”. Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”. If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer, as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing. But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. items.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
items.summary: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

items.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots. Continue reading...
